questions.q: Which sentence describes a client and a server?
questions.explain: The client asks and the server answers. A browser, a phone app and curl are all clients. The backend you build is a server.
options: The client stores the data; the server shows it on the screen
The client sends a request; the server waits for requests and sends back a response
The client is always a browser; the server is always a phone
They are two names for the same program

questions.q: A web page shows ten images. At least how many requests does the browser make to show it?
questions.explain: One request gets one response. The browser asks once for the page, then once for each image: 1 + 10 = 11.

questions.q: What is an IP address?
questions.explain: Every computer on the internet has an IP address, such as 104.20.23.154. The name example.com is a domain name, which DNS turns into an IP address.
options: The name of a website, like example.com
A number that says where a computer is on the internet, like a postal address
The password of your Wi-Fi network
The path of a page, like /tasks

questions.q: Which of these is a valid IPv4 address?
questions.explain: IPv4 is four numbers from 0 to 255. 300 is too big, and three numbers are too few. The form with colons is IPv6.

questions.q: Why does IPv6 exist?
questions.explain: IPv4 has a limited number of addresses and they ran out. IPv6 is a longer form with far more of them.
options: The world ran out of IPv4 addresses, and IPv6 has many more

questions.q: What does DNS do?
questions.explain: DNS, the Domain Name System, looks up a name like example.com and returns its IP addresses. Encryption is HTTPS's job, and the port picks the program.
options: Encrypts the connection between browser and server
Turns a domain name into an IP address, like a phone book
Picks which program on a computer gets the request
Stores the data of your application

questions.q: nslookup example.com shows several addresses for one name. Why do big sites have several?
questions.explain: If one machine fails, clients can use another address. Your answers can also differ from someone else's: the numbers change over time and between countries.
options: Each address shows a different website
So that one broken machine does not take the site down
One address is for images, the other for text

questions.q: You start a server on your own computer while developing. Which address reaches it?
questions.explain: localhost always means "this computer", and its IPv4 address is 127.0.0.1. It is how you reach servers running on your own machine.

questions.q: One computer runs a web server and a database. How does a request reach the right program?
questions.explain: The IP address finds the computer. The port, a number from 1 to 65535, finds the program on it.

questions.q: Which port does https://shop.example.com/cart use?
questions.explain: The URL names no port, so the default for https is used: 443. The default for plain http is 80.

questions.q: Which port is the standard one for PostgreSQL, the database used later in the course?
questions.explain: PostgreSQL listens on 5432. 80 and 443 are for the web, and 3000 or 8080 are common choices for your own server while you develop.

questions.q: In https://api.example.com/tasks?done=false&limit=10, which part is the query?
questions.explain: The query comes after ? and holds options as name=value pairs joined by &. /tasks is the path and api.example.com is the hostname.

questions.q: What does the HTTP method GET say?
questions.explain: GET asks for something. POST means "here is something new". The method, the path and the headers together describe what the client wants.

questions.q: Which three parts does an HTTP response have?
questions.explain: A response starts with a status code (how it went), then headers (extra information), then the body: the page, image or data. Method and path belong to the request.
options: A method, a path and a query
A status code, headers and a body
An IP address, a port and a domain
A protocol, a hostname and a port

questions.q: What do the status codes 200 and 404 mean?
questions.explain: 200 means success. 404 means the server does not know the path you asked for.
options: 200: OK, here it is; 404: not found
200: a GET request; 404: a POST request

questions.q: What does curl -I https://example.com print?
questions.explain: With -I, curl asks only for the status line and headers. Without it, curl prints the body, the HTML of the page.
options: Only the HTML of the page
Only the status and the headers
The IP address of the server

questions.q: You are in Windows PowerShell and want the real curl. What do you type?
questions.explain: In Windows PowerShell, plain curl is a different command with different options. curl.exe is the real curl, which comes with Windows 10 and 11.

questions.q: A response has the header content-type: application/json. What is in its body?
questions.explain: The content-type header says what the body is. text/html is a web page; application/json is data, typical for an API.
options: A web page for people to read
Data in JSON format, made for programs

questions.q: What does HTTPS add to HTTP?
questions.explain: HTTPS sends HTTP through an encrypted TLS connection, so nobody on the way can read or change it. The certificate proves the server's identity: that is the padlock.
options: Faster pages, because data is compressed
An encrypted connection, and a certificate that proves the server really is who it says
A way to use domain names instead of IP addresses

questions.q: Your login form will be used by real people. Which address should it send the password to?
questions.explain: Plain HTTP travels as readable text, so anyone on the same network or on the way can read it. Every public site and API must use HTTPS. Plain HTTP is only acceptable on localhost.
options: http://api.myapp.com/login, if the Wi-Fi has a password
Either one, as long as the password is long

questions.q: When is plain http:// acceptable?
questions.explain: On localhost, the request never travels over a network, so nobody can read it. Everything that real users reach must use HTTPS.
options: For any page that has no images
For APIs, because programs are not people
On localhost, where the data never leaves your computer
For login forms on small websites

questions.q: Where in the browser can you see every request a page makes, with its method, status code and headers?
questions.explain: Open the devtools with F12, choose Network and reload the page. Each row is one request; click it to see the details.
options: The Console tab of the devtools
The Network tab of the devtools

questions.q: What is a web API?
questions.explain: A web page is made for people; an API is made for programs. It usually answers with JSON, a text format for data that looks like JavaScript objects.
options: A web page with nice colours
A set of URLs that programs call to read or change data, usually answering in JSON
The program that turns names into IP addresses
A database that runs in the browser

questions.q: The tiny API calls server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1"). What does that mean?
questions.explain: Port 0 means "any free port"; the operating system picks one. 127.0.0.1 is localhost, so only your own computer can reach the server.
options: Listen on port 0 only, reachable from the whole internet
Use any free port, and accept connections only from this computer

questions.q: The tiny API keeps its tasks in a list inside the program. What is the problem with that for a real app?
questions.explain: Real data must survive restarts and be shared by many copies of the server. That is what a database is for: a separate program built to store data safely and find it fast.
options: Lists cannot hold more than two tasks
The tasks are gone when the program stops, and other copies of the server cannot share them
Lists make the server use HTTP instead of HTTPS

questions.q: In a well-built app, who does the browser talk to?
questions.explain: The browser never talks to the database directly. The backend stands between them, checks each request and who is asking, and only then reads or changes data.
options: Directly to the database, because it is faster
To the database and the backend, equally
Only to the backend, which talks to the database and decides what each person may read or change

questions.q: Someone opens a task app. What happens first?
questions.explain: The browser first needs an address: DNS turns the domain into an IP address. Then it connects on port 443, sets up HTTPS and only then sends the HTTP request.
options: The backend asks the database for the tasks
The browser asks DNS for the IP address of the app's domain

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The hostname is the name only, without the port. The URL names port 8443. The path stops before the ?; the rest is the query.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: url.protocol includes the colon at the end: https:.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The URL names no port, so port is empty. The client then uses the protocol's default, 443 for https. JSON.stringify shows the empty text as "".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: search is the whole query, starting with ?. searchParams.get("limit") gives just the value of one option.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: get("q") finds milk. The query has no page option, and get returns null for a missing name.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: This URL names a port, 3000, so port is not empty. new URL does not do a DNS lookup, so the hostname stays localhost.
questions.code:
const url = new URL("http://localhost:3000/search?q=milk");
console.log(url.hostname, url.port, url.pathname);

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: host includes the port when the URL names one; hostname is only the name. DNS looks up the hostname.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: + with a text joins, so the number 3000 is added as text. The same happens with "/tasks". This is how the tiny API builds its base address.

questions.q: A server sends data as JSON text. What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify turns an object into JSON text: names in double quotes, no spaces. Numbers and true/false stay without quotes.
questions.code:
const task = { id: 1, title: "Buy milk", done: false };
console.log(JSON.stringify(task));

questions.q: A client receives JSON text. What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.parse turns JSON text back into a JavaScript object, so you can read its properties. This is what response.json() does for you.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The list has two tasks. Positions start at 0, so tasks[1] is the second one, "Write report".

questions.q: Run this with Node.js. What does it print?
questions.explain: The server checks the method and path. GET /tasks matches and gets 200. Any other path falls through to the 404 answer. One request, one response each.

questions.q: Run this with Node.js. What does it print?
questions.explain: The server set status 200 and the content-type header. response.json() turns the JSON text back into an object, which Node prints as { status: 'ok' }.

questions.q: Use new URL(...) to print the hostname, the port, the path and the value of q for http://localhost:3000/search?q=milk, one per line.
questions.explain: Use url.hostname, url.port, url.pathname and url.searchParams.get("q"). The port is not empty because the URL names it.
questions.starter:
const url = new URL("http://localhost:3000/search?q=milk");
// print hostname, port, path and the value of q

questions.q: Finish realPort: return the port the client really connects to. If the URL names a port, return it as a number. If not, return 443 for https: and 80 for http:. The program should print 443 80 8080.
questions.explain: When a URL names no port, url.port is empty, and the protocol's default is used. Remember that url.protocol ends with a colon: "https:".

questions.q: Finish taskUrl so it builds a local address from a port and a path. taskUrl(3000, "/tasks") should return "http://localhost:3000/tasks".
questions.explain: Join the pieces with + (or a template literal): protocol and host, a colon, the port, then the path. The path already starts with /.

questions.q: Finish isSafeForPasswords: return true when the URL uses https:, or when it is plain http: on the hostname localhost. Return false otherwise. The program should print true true false.
questions.explain: HTTPS is always required for real users. Plain HTTP is only acceptable on localhost, where the data never leaves your computer.

questions.q: Finish readOptions so it prints the values of done and limit from the URL's query, like done: false and limit: 10, one per line.
questions.explain: url.searchParams.get(name) reads one option from the query. The values come back as text, like "10".

questions.q: Finish topLevel so it returns the last part of a hostname. Hint: "a.b.c".split(".") gives the pieces. topLevel("api.example.com") should return "com".
questions.explain: split(".") cuts the name at every dot. The last piece is at position parts.length - 1, because positions start at 0.

questions.q: Finish countParts so it returns how many numbers are in an IP address written with dots. Hint: split at ".". The program should print 4 3.
questions.explain: split(".") gives one piece per number, and .length counts them. A real IPv4 address has exactly four numbers, so 104.20.23 is not complete.

questions.q: An API answers in JSON. Turn the health object into JSON text with JSON.stringify and print it. The output must be {"status":"ok"}.
questions.explain: JSON.stringify turns an object into JSON text, the format APIs send. Printing the object directly would show { status: 'ok' }, which is not JSON.
questions.starter:
const health = { status: "ok" };
// print health as JSON text
